author: BrentDesk Staff
headline: Gulf exhibitor lists require two-language verification
deck: Arabic and English releases render company names differently, and the official floor list is the authority.
excerpt: Exhibitor names at Gulf trade shows appear in different transliterations between Arabic and English releases, making the organiser's official list the reference point.
content:
A practical note from covering the Saudi Warehousing and Logistics Expo in Riyadh this week, and one that applies across regional trade coverage.

Company names released in Arabic and in English do not always match in their Latin-script rendering. Arabic names transliterated into English have no single correct form, and different translators, agencies and company registrations make different choices. A firm may itself use one spelling in its trade name, another in its commercial registration and a third in its English marketing material.

The practical consequence is that assembling an exhibitor list from more than one source requires verification rather than compilation. A buyer searching for a supplier encountered at a show may not locate it under the spelling they noted. A database matching exhibitors against a customer list will produce both duplicates and misses. And a publication printing a name in an unfamiliar form has misnamed a company.

The reliable approach is narrow. Use the company's own English name as it appears on its own materials, and where that is unavailable, note the ambiguity rather than choosing between renderings. The official exhibitor list published by the organiser is the authority for who was present.

The same consideration extends beyond company names. Event names, venue names and government body names all carry multiple English renderings, and September's Gulf calendar has produced several. IFM Expo, the industrial facilities management exhibition that ran at Dhahran Expo from 8 to 10 September, and the Saudi Facility Management Association's forum at Riyadh's convention centre from 20 September are separate events with different organisers, cities and audiences, and this publication has covered the distinction between them.

None of this reflects on organisers working in two languages under deadline. It is an argument for treating a press release as a starting point for verification rather than as a verified record, particularly where a name is about to appear in print alongside a claim about what a company does.

Named exhibitors reported for the Riyadh show include SAL Logistics, Almajdouie, Swisslog, SSI Schäfer and Kardex, each appearing consistently across sources. The exhibition drew more than 350 exhibitors from over 25 countries showing upwards of 4,000 products and services.

For readers using trade show coverage commercially, the same principle applies to figures as to names: attribute them to the party that published them, and note whether they are projections or counts.

The same care applies to venue and hall detail. Several Gulf events changed dates or venues during 2026, and organiser homepages carry the current position while other listings follow later.
